source_text: XVII. Καὶ πρὸς αὐτὸν Ῥουφῖνός τις παρεστὼς τῶν ἐν τῇ ῥητορικῇ διαφέρειν δοκούντων εἶπεν· Παῦσαι, Πιόνιε, μὴ κενοδόξει. ὁ δὲ πρὸς αὐτόν· Ἀραί σου αἱ ῥητορεῖαι; ταῦτά σου τὰ βιβλία; ταῦτα Σωκράτης ὑπὸ Ἀνύτου οὐκ ἔπαθεν. νῦν πάντες Ἄνυτοι καὶ Μέλητοι. ἄρα Σωκράτης καὶ Ἀριστείδης καὶ Ἀνάξαρχος καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ ἐκενοδόξουν καθ᾽ ὑμᾶς, ὅτι καὶ φιλοσοφίαν καὶ δικαιοσύνην καὶ καρτερίαν ἤσκησαν; ὁ δὲ Ῥουφῖνος ἀκούσας οὕτως ἐσιώπησεν.
pass_a_gloss: And a certain Rufinus who was standing by him, one of those reputed to excel in rhetoric, said: Cease, Pionius, do not be empty-glorying. And he to him: Curses to your rhetorics; are these things from your books; these things Socrates suffered under Anytus; now all are Anytuses and Meletuses; then were Socrates and Aristides and Anaxarchus and the rest empty-glorying according to you, because they practiced philosophy and justice and endurance? And Rufinus having heard thus fell silent.
pass_b_english: Then a bystander named Rufinus, who was counted among those supposed to excel in rhetoric, said to him, Stop it, Pionius, stop your vainglory.
But Pionius said back to him, Away with your rhetoric!
Such things Socrates never suffered at the hands of Anytus — yet now everyone plays Anytus and Meletus.
Were Socrates and Aristides and Anaxarchus and the rest, then, vainglorious in your eyes, because they gave themselves to philosophy and justice and steadfast endurance?
When Rufinus heard this answer, he fell silent.

choices.why: present imperative with μή forbids continuing conduct, not a single act, and targets empty-glory motive
plural abstract with dative/genitive of disadvantage is an imprecation rejecting Rufinus's art, not a question about books
kata with accusative gives the standard of judgment, answering Rufinus's charge
